title: The Christmas Truce of 1914
text:
By December 1914 the war that was supposed to be over by Christmas had settled into lines of muddy, freezing trenches across Belgium and France. In places the British and German lines were only a few dozen meters apart.

On Christmas Eve, along stretches of the front in Flanders, British soldiers saw small Christmas trees with candles appear on the German parapets and heard the Germans singing carols. The British answered with their own. Men began shouting greetings across no man's land. At dawn on Christmas Day, in many sectors, soldiers climbed out of the trenches unarmed and walked toward each other.

Their letters home describe what followed. They shook hands, exchanged cigarettes, chocolate, buttons and souvenirs, showed each other photographs of their families and took pictures together. Both sides used the quiet to bury their dead lying between the lines, sometimes in joint services. In some places men kicked a football around. In some sectors the truce lasted days.

It was never official, and commanders on both sides disapproved. Orders went out to prevent any repeat, and later Christmases saw no truce on that scale. The war went on for nearly four more years.
lesson: Even deep enmity hides a shared humanity that can surface when people meet face to face. Remember that those on the other side are people too.
people: British and German soldiers on the Western Front
location: Western Front, Flanders (Belgium) and northern France
source: Soldiers' letters and diaries; Malcolm Brown and Shirley Seaton, Christmas Truce (1984)
caveat: The truce was patchy and did not happen everywhere, and reports of organized football matches are less certain than the fraternization itself.
